narrative:
The model predicted an 82.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These consistently low academic standings signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the demands of the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor and also contributed toward predicting failure. At 28, it sits well below the average of 37 among accepted students, further lowering the outlook for passing the bar.

Other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 2.10 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), lower-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and were not decisive.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score. Consider targeted test preparation, academic support programs, or additional coursework before reapplying. These steps can directly address the factors that led to this outcome. (218 words)
